slides.heading: Climate Tipping Points
slides.body: The thresholds where small changes trigger massive, irreversible shifts in Earth's systems

slides.heading: What Is a Tipping Point?
slides.body: A climate tipping point is a threshold beyond which a part of Earth's system self-reinforces into a new state — independent of further human emissions. Think of it like a ball rolling off a hill: once it passes the edge, it falls on its own.

slides.heading: The Greenland Ice Sheet
slides.body: If Greenland's ice melts past a critical point, the sheet could collapse entirely over centuries, raising sea levels by 7 meters. Scientists estimate this tipping point may be crossed between 1.5°C and 2°C of global warming.

slides.heading: The Amazon Dieback
slides.body: The Amazon rainforest generates its own rainfall. As deforestation and drought reduce forest cover, rainfall drops — causing more forest to die. Studies suggest 20–25% deforestation could flip parts of the Amazon into savanna permanently.

slides.heading: Permafrost and Methane
slides.body: Arctic permafrost stores twice the carbon currently in the atmosphere. As it thaws, microbes release methane — a greenhouse gas 80x more potent than CO₂ in the short term. This creates a feedback loop that accelerates warming far beyond our control.

slides.heading: The Atlantic Circulation (AMOC)
slides.body: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation moves warm water north and regulates Europe's climate. It has already weakened significantly. If it collapses, Europe could face severe cooling, shifting monsoons, and rising seas along the US East Coast.

slides.heading: Tipping Points Can Cascade
slides.body: The most alarming finding: tipping points are interconnected. The Amazon's collapse could weaken African monsoons. Greenland's melt could stall Atlantic circulation. A 2022 study found that at 2°C of warming, five major tipping points could trigger simultaneously.

slides.heading: How Close Are We?
slides.body: Earth has already warmed approximately 1.3°C above pre-industrial levels. Some scientists warn that tipping points for the Greenland ice sheet, West Antarctic ice, and tropical coral reefs may already be closer than current models predict.

slides.heading: Why This Changes the Math
slides.body: Traditional climate projections assumed gradual, proportional change. Tipping points reveal that climate risk is not linear — it is lumpy and irreversible. A world at 1.6°C may be qualitatively safer than a world at 1.7°C, depending on which thresholds lie between them.

slides.heading: The Case for Urgency
slides.body: Understanding tipping points transforms climate action from a gradual economic optimization into a race against irreversibility. Every fraction of a degree we avoid is not just an improvement — it may be the difference between a recoverable and an unrecoverable world.
